source: OECD monetary aggregates (broad money, licence CC BY 4.0; this is an adaptation, not the OECD's view) for the 28 economies the OECD covers, the IMF depository corporations survey for the rest, both converted with the IMF's end-of-month exchange rates; the sums are our calculation
note: This adds up the money people and companies hold in every economy with a figure, turned into US dollars at each month's exchange rate. Each country counts money its own way, so the total mixes definitions; and a change in dollars includes currency moves, so read a country's growth in its own currency in its own book. The euro area is counted once, as a whole. Money is never added to debt: a bank loan and the deposit it creates are the same dollar. 129 economies are in the first month and 110 in the last, so part of the rise over time is economies joining the data. In June 2026, 46 economies (3.5% of the total) show their latest earlier figure. Years left out because the dollar amount fails the check against the IMF's own dollar GDP (usually a currency unit that differs between two IMF tables, or a redenomination): Democratic Republic of the Congo 2000-2002; Guinea-Bissau 2003; Myanmar 2001-2012; Sudan 2021; Somalia 2018; South Sudan 2015; Syria 2011; Zimbabwe 2021-2024. A country's last figure is carried up to six months, and the book ends at the latest month with figures for the United States, the euro area, China and Japan. Sources: OECD, International Monetary Fund.
